evidence.claim: A freeway through wooded hills, with trains sharing the corridor.
evidence.quote: It lies in Alameda County, where it is highly urban, and Contra Costa County, where it passes through wooded hillsides and suburbs.

evidence.claim: with trains sharing the corridor.

evidence.quote: Contra Costa County, where it passes through wooded hillsides and suburbs.

evidence.claim: It is a freeway throughout, with BART trains in the median except near the tunnel and the approach to Interstate 680.
evidence.quote: The Yellow Line of the Bay Area Rapid Transit (BART) system runs in the freeway's center median, excepting the vicinity of the Caldecott Tunnel and the approach to the interchange with Interstate 680.

evidence.claim: Caltrans has designated the stretch from the tunnel’s eastern end to I-680 as a scenic highway.
evidence.quote: Caltrans has only designated it as a scenic highway between the eastern end of the Caldecott Tunnel and I-680

evidence.claim: It is a freeway throughout
evidence.quote: A freeway throughout its entire length

evidence.claim: The road’s passage through the hills took decades to secure: an 1871 private tunneling attempt led by L.W. Kennedy struck water after about 200 feet and washed out.
evidence.quote: It was revived in 1871 in a private attempt led by L.W. Kennedy which however failed after boring about 200 feet into the hills from the east side of the hills above the location of today's Caldecott Tunnel when water was struck, washing out the work.

evidence.claim: Alameda and Contra Costa counties formed Joint Highway District 13 in 1929 to replace the inadequate existing tunnel.
evidence.quote: In November 1926, the Counties of Alameda and Contra Costa, and the City of Oakland agreed to the construction of a new tunnel through the Berkeley Hills to replace the old, small, decrepit and increasingly inadequate existing tunnel. In 1929, Alameda and Contra Costa County formed Joint Highway District 13 to accomplish this goal.

evidence.claim: The new twin bores opened in 1937.
evidence.quote: Named after Thomas E. Caldecott, former mayor of Berkeley, it opened in 1937 as a two-bore tunnel.

evidence.claim: By 1960, a freeway eastern approach had helped accelerate Contra Costa County’s change from agricultural community to major suburb.
evidence.quote: By 1960, the Division of Highways had rebuilt the eastern approach to the tunnel into a freeway. With Contra Costa County accessible by freeway, its change from an agricultural community into a major suburb accelerated.

evidence.claim: From the east portal, the highway crosses unincorporated land before entering Orinda.
evidence.quote: On the other side of the tunnel, SR 24 travels through unincorporated Contra Costa County before entering Orinda.

evidence.claim: Rolling, oak-covered hills frame the city.
evidence.quote: framed by its rolling oak-covered hills

evidence.claim: Continue east into Lafayette, where the freeway crosses the Mokelumne Aqueduct soon after entering town.
evidence.quote: SR 24 crosses the Mokelumne Aqueduct soon after entering the city of Lafayette.

evidence.claim: The drive ends at I-680 just inside Walnut Creek, where Route 24 itself terminates.
evidence.quote: SR 24 terminates at the intersection with Interstate 680 just inside the city limits of Walnut Creek.

evidence.claim: The two oldest Caldecott bores carry eastbound traffic; the newer pair carries westbound traffic.
evidence.quote: Currently, the two oldest bores carry eastbound traffic and the two newest bores carry westbound traffic.

evidence.claim: That arrangement replaced a daily balancing act.
evidence.quote: When the fourth bore was opened to traffic, the need for the daily traffic reversal was eliminated

evidence.claim: After the third bore opened in 1964, the middle bore could reverse direction to give commuters four lanes in the heavier direction.
evidence.quote: The new third bore made it possible to provide four lanes to accommodate the heavier commute-direction traffic by reversing the traffic flow of the middle bore.

evidence.claim: Plastic lane markers rose from tubes in the pavement when filled with water, helping separate traffic.
evidence.quote: Plastic lane delineators were set in tubes within the pavement. With the touch of a button, water would fill tubes to cause the delineators to pop up from the pavement

evidence.claim: The fourth bore, completed in 2013, ended that daily reversal.
evidence.quote: Bore 4 (the northernmost bore), completed in 2013

evidence.claim: The tunnel bears the name of Thomas E. Caldecott, a former Berkeley mayor and president of the highway district that built the first pair.
evidence.quote: It is named after Thomas E. Caldecott (1878–1951), who was mayor of Berkeley in 1930–1932, a member of the Alameda County Board of Supervisors in 1933–1945, and president of Joint Highway District 13, which built the first two bores.

evidence.claim: After the third bore opened in 1964
evidence.quote: The third bore opened in 1964

evidence.claim: Orinda’s oak-covered hills once held a rural landscape known for ranching and summer cabins.
evidence.quote: The area was originally rural, mainly known for ranching and summer cabins.

evidence.claim: In 1876, County Sheriff William Walker Camron bought land east of the Berkeley Hills and named it Orinda Park.
evidence.quote: In 1876, County Sheriff William Walker Camron bought a tract of land east of the Berkeley Hills.  His wife, Alice Marsh Camron, loved the poetry of  Katherine Philips, who was known as the "Matchless Orinda".  Camron named his new tract of land "Orinda Park".

evidence.claim: His wife, Alice Marsh Camron, admired Katherine Philips, the poet known as the Matchless Orinda.
evidence.quote: His wife, Alice Marsh Camron, loved the poetry of  Katherine Philips, who was known as the "Matchless Orinda".

evidence.claim: Year-round residence became more popular after the Caldecott opened in 1937 and eased travel west.
evidence.quote: Orinda's popularity as a year-round residence grew after the 1937 completion of the Caldecott Tunnel, which provided easier access to the west.

evidence.claim: BART service reached Orinda in 1973, after completion of its separate Berkeley Hills Tunnel.
evidence.quote: Service at the station began on May 21, 1973

evidence.claim: Its island platform sits in Route 24’s median.
evidence.quote: The station has an island platform in the center median of State Route 24.

evidence.claim: In 1857, Benjamin Shreve proposed Centerville, then suggested La Fayette after learning that California already had a post office with his first choice.
evidence.quote: In 1857 Benjamin Shreve, owner and manager of a roadside hotel-general store (which faced today's Lafayette Plaza), applied for a post office for the community, first requesting the name Centerville. When informed that a post office with that name already existed in California, Shreve suggested La Fayette

evidence.claim: The agricultural village became a commuter town in the mid-twentieth century.
evidence.quote: In the mid-1900s, Lafayette was transformed from an agricultural village into a commuter town
